questions.q: Name the four whorls of a typical angiosperm flower in correct acropetal order (from base to apex) and state the primary function of each whorl in one phrase.
questions.a: Correct answer: Calyx (sepals) – protection of bud; Corolla (petals) – attraction of pollinators; Androecium (stamens) – production of male gametes (pollen); Gynoecium (carpels) – production and protection of female gametes (ovules). A wrong answer (e.g., swapping androecium/gynoecium order or assigning photosynthesis to petals) reveals confusion between vegetative and reproductive roles or misunderstanding of acropetal succession on the thalamus.

questions.q: A flower has both androecium and gynoecium but lacks corolla. Is it a complete flower? Is it a bisexual flower? Explain the difference between the two terms.
questions.a: Correct answer: It is an incomplete flower (missing one or more whorls) but a bisexual flower (has both male and female reproductive organs). "Complete" refers to presence of all four whorls; "bisexual" refers only to presence of both androecium and gynoecium. A student who says "it is incomplete therefore unisexual" conflates morphological completeness with sexual condition — a common error because both terms describe "what is present" but at different organizational levels.

questions.q: In a longitudinal section of a flower, you observe that the thalamus is cup-shaped and the ovary sits at the bottom of the cup with sepals, petals, and stamens attached to the rim. What is the position of the ovary? How does this position affect the type of fruit that will develop?
questions.a: Correct answer: The ovary is inferior (epigynous flower). The thalamus grows upward and fuses with the ovary wall, so the fruit that develops will be an inferior ovary fruit (e.g., apple, where the fleshy part is swollen thalamus, not ovary). A wrong answer like "superior ovary" or "fruit type unchanged" shows failure to visualize 3D floral architecture and its consequence for fruit morphology — a frequent board exam diagram-labeling trap.

questions.q: Compare the floral formulae of Brassicaceae (⊕ ♂♀ K4 C4 A2+4 G(2)) and Fabaceae (↑ ♂♀ K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G1). Identify two structural differences in androecium and gynoecium that reflect their distinct pollination strategies.
questions.a: Correct answer: Brassicaceae has tetradynamous stamens (2+4) and a syncarpous bicarpellary ovary with parietal placentation; Fabaceae has diadelphous stamens (9+1) and a monocarpellary ovary with marginal placentation. Tetradynamous stamens ensure pollen deposition on specific pollinator body parts; diadelphous stamens form a keel that triggers explosive pollen release. A student who only notes "different numbers" misses the functional morphology linking androecium cohesion to pollination mechanism — a NEET-level application.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "In a zygomorphic flower, the calyx is always bilabiate and the corolla is always papilionaceous." Is it correct? If not, correct it with a counterexample.
questions.a: Correct answer: The statement is false. Zygomorphy means the flower can be divided into two equal halves only in one vertical plane. Bilabiate calyx (e.g., Salvia) and papilionaceous corolla (e.g., pea) are two specific types of zygomorphic flowers, but not universal. Counterexample: Orchid flowers are zygomorphic but have neither bilabiate calyx nor papilionaceous corolla — they have highly modified perianth (tepals) and a specialized labellum. A student who agrees reveals overgeneralization from textbook examples without understanding the definition of zygomorphy.

questions.q: Design a simple field observation to distinguish between a hypogynous, perigynous, and epigynous flower using only a hand lens and a scalpel. List the steps and the key feature you would record for each type.
questions.a: Expected answer: Step 1: Pick a fresh flower. Step 2: Make a longitudinal section through the thalamus. Step 3: Observe the point of attachment of sepals, petals, and stamens relative to the ovary. Key feature: Hypogynous — all whorls attached below a superior ovary (e.g., mustard); Perigynous — whorls attached on the rim of a cup-shaped thalamus surrounding a half-inferior ovary (e.g., rose); Epigynous — whorls attached above an inferior ovary, thalamus fused to ovary wall (e.g., apple). A poor answer that only describes "ovary position" without the sectioning step shows lack of practical anatomical skill — a common gap in lab-based board questions.
